Leviticus 1.summary: The LORD calls to Moses from the tabernacle and explains how an Israelite may bring a burnt offering (Leviticus 1:1–2). A bull from the herd must be a male without blemish; the worshiper lays his hand on its head, and the priests sprinkle its blood and burn the whole animal on the altar (Leviticus 1:3–9). A sheep or goat is offered the same way (Leviticus 1:10–13), and a poorer worshiper may bring turtledoves or young pigeons (Leviticus 1:14–17). Each one is burned as "a sweet savour unto the LORD."
Leviticus 1.whereWeAre: Exodus ended with God's glory filling the newly built tabernacle. Now God speaks to Moses from that tent and explains how people may come near him. This chapter covers the burnt offering, the first of five offerings described in chapters 1–7.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Speaks these laws to Moses from the tabernacle.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Hears the LORD's words and passes them on to Israel.

keyFigures.name: Aaron's sons, the priests
keyFigures.role: Sprinkle the blood and burn the offering on the altar.

keyThemes.explanation: God himself shows the way to come before him at the tabernacle.
The whole animal is burned on the altar. Nothing is held back.
A bull, a sheep or goat, or two birds: everyone can bring something.

Leviticus 2.summary: God gives instructions for offerings made from fine flour, oil, and frankincense, or bread prepared in different ways. The priest burns a handful as a memorial, and the rest belongs to Aaron and his sons as most holy food (Leviticus 2:1–10). Every offering is seasoned with salt, no leaven or honey may be burned on the altar, and firstfruits of grain are offered roasted (Leviticus 2:11–16). The chapter shows that Israelite worship includes produce and labor as well as animals.
Leviticus 2.whereWeAre: Chapter 1 described the burnt offering of an animal. This chapter turns to the grain offering, made from flour, oil, and frankincense. Chapter 3 continues with the peace offering.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Speaks these laws to Moses from the tabernacle.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Hears the LORD's words and passes them on to Israel.

keyFigures.name: Aaron and his sons
keyFigures.role: Burn a handful of the grain offering and eat the rest as holy food.

keyThemes.explanation: Flour, oil, and baked bread can all be offered to God.
Most of the grain offering feeds the priests who serve.
Every offering is seasoned with "the salt of the covenant," a sign of a lasting promise.

Leviticus 3.summary: The LORD describes the peace offering, brought from the cattle, sheep, or goats. Male or female animals without defect may be brought. Worshipers lay hands on the offering; priests apply its blood to the altar and burn specified fat portions (Leviticus 3:1–16). The chapter ends with a lasting rule: "eat neither fat nor blood" (Leviticus 3:17). These offerings celebrate peace with God; chapter 7 explains the shared meal that goes with them.
Leviticus 3.whereWeAre: After the burnt offering in chapter 1 and the grain offering in chapter 2, this chapter describes the peace offering, a sacrifice shared as a meal. Chapter 4 moves from offerings of worship and thanks to offerings for sin.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Speaks these laws to Moses from the tabernacle.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Hears the LORD's words and passes them on to Israel.

keyFigures.name: Aaron's sons, the priests
keyFigures.role: Sprinkle the blood and burn the fat on the altar.

keyThemes.explanation: The peace offering celebrates being at peace with God, and most of it is eaten in a shared meal.
"All the fat is the LORD's." The best part goes on the altar.
Israel must never eat blood.

Leviticus 4.summary: God gives the sin offering for anyone who sins "through ignorance" against one of his commands (Leviticus 4:1–2). An anointed priest who sins brings a young bull, and its blood is sprinkled before the veil (Leviticus 4:3–12). If the whole congregation sins, the elders bring a young bull for the people (Leviticus 4:13–21). A ruler brings a male goat (Leviticus 4:22–26), and an ordinary person brings a female goat or lamb (Leviticus 4:27–35). Each time the priest makes an atonement, "and it shall be forgiven him."
Leviticus 4.whereWeAre: The first three offerings in chapters 1–3 were gifts of worship. Now God explains the sin offering, for someone who breaks a command without meaning to. Chapter 5 gives more cases and begins the trespass offering.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Gives the sin offering for sins done through ignorance.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Hears the LORD's words and passes them on to Israel.

keyFigures.name: The priest
keyFigures.role: Sprinkles the blood and makes an atonement for the one who sinned.

keyThemes.explanation: Even sins people did not know they were doing must be dealt with.
A priest's sin needs a costlier offering than an ordinary person's, because it affects the whole people.
Again and again God promises, "it shall be forgiven him."

Leviticus 5.summary: A person who fails to testify, touches something unclean, or swears a rash oath must confess and bring a sin offering (Leviticus 5:1–6). People unable to bring a lamb or goat may bring birds, or in still greater poverty a flour offering (Leviticus 5:7–13). The chapter then addresses misuse of holy things and other violations requiring a ram as a trespass offering, including restitution plus one-fifth when sacred property is wronged (Leviticus 5:14–19).
Leviticus 5.whereWeAre: Chapter 4 covered the sin offering for sins done without meaning to. This chapter gives more examples, lets poor people bring smaller offerings, and begins the trespass offering. Chapter 6 finishes the trespass laws and turns to the priests' duties.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Gives the laws for the sin offering and the trespass offering.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Hears the LORD's words and passes them on to Israel.

keyFigures.name: The priest
keyFigures.role: Makes an atonement for the guilty person.

keyThemes.explanation: The guilty person must "confess that he hath sinned."
Those who cannot afford a lamb bring birds, and the poorest bring a little flour.
Wrongs must be repaid in full, with a fifth added.

Leviticus 6.summary: The trespass offering also covers cheating, theft, keeping lost property, and lying under oath; offenders must return what they took plus a fifth and present a ram (Leviticus 6:1–7). God then instructs the priests to keep the altar fire burning, remove ashes properly, and handle the grain offerings and sin offerings as holy food (Leviticus 6:8–30). The chapter pairs making things right with others and the priests' careful care of the altar.
Leviticus 6.whereWeAre: Chapters 1–5 told the people what to bring. Here the focus turns to the priests and how they handle each offering, starting with the altar: "The fire shall ever be burning upon the altar; it shall never go out" (Leviticus 6:13). These instructions for the priests finish in chapter 7.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Speaks these laws to Moses from the tabernacle.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Is told, "Command Aaron and his sons."

keyFigures.name: Aaron and his sons
keyFigures.role: Keep the altar fire burning and eat the priests' share of the offerings.

keyThemes.explanation: A cheat or thief must return what he took and add a fifth.
"The fire shall ever be burning upon the altar; it shall never go out."
The sin offering is "most holy," so even the pots it touches must be cleaned.

Leviticus 7.summary: The LORD finishes the instructions for the trespass and peace offerings. Rules identify portions reserved for priests and distinguish thanksgiving, vow, and freewill offerings, including how quickly their meat must be eaten (Leviticus 7:1–21). Eating blood or the fat designated for sacrifice remains prohibited; the breast and the right shoulder belong to the priests (Leviticus 7:22–36). The chapter ends by summing up all the offering laws (Leviticus 7:37–38).
Leviticus 7.whereWeAre: This chapter finishes the priests' instructions for the offerings that began in chapter 6. It explains which parts the priests may eat and closes the offering laws of chapters 1–7. In chapter 8 the priests who will carry out these laws are ordained.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Speaks these laws to Moses from the tabernacle.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Hears the LORD's words and passes them on to Israel.

keyFigures.name: Aaron and his sons
keyFigures.role: Receive the breast and the right shoulder as their share.

keyThemes.explanation: A peace offering can give thanks, keep a vow, or be a free gift.
The meat must be eaten on time and only by those who are clean.
The breast and the right shoulder belong to the priests.

Leviticus 8.summary: Moses assembles the community at the tent entrance, washes and clothes Aaron and his sons, and anoints the sanctuary and Aaron (Leviticus 8:1–13). He offers the sin offering, the burnt offering, and "the ram of consecration"; blood and oil mark the priests, and they eat the ordination meal (Leviticus 8:14–32). They must remain at the tent entrance for seven days and obey the commissioning instructions (Leviticus 8:33–36).
Leviticus 8.whereWeAre: The offering laws are complete in chapters 1–7, but Israel still has no priests to carry them out. Moses now ordains Aaron and his sons, just as God commanded in Exodus 29. The seven-day ceremony leads into the priests' first day of service in chapter 9.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Commands the ordination of the priests.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Washes, clothes, and anoints Aaron and his sons and offers the sacrifices.

keyFigures.name: Aaron
keyFigures.role: Dressed in the holy garments and anointed as high priest.

keyFigures.name: Aaron's sons
keyFigures.role: Clothed and set apart with their father.

keyFigures.name: The congregation
keyFigures.role: Gathers at the door of the tabernacle to watch.

keyThemes.explanation: Aaron and his sons are washed, dressed, and anointed in front of the whole people.
Blood is put on the priests' right ear, thumb, and toe before they serve.
The priests stay at the door of the tabernacle for seven days, as God commanded.

Leviticus 9.summary: On the eighth day after ordination, Moses directs Aaron and Israel’s elders to bring offerings (Leviticus 9:1–7). Aaron presents sacrifices for himself and the people, and Moses and Aaron bless the congregation (Leviticus 9:8–23). The LORD’s glory appears, fire comes out from before the LORD and consumes the altar offering, and the people shout and fall facedown (Leviticus 9:23–24). God shows that he accepts the new priests and their worship.
Leviticus 9.whereWeAre: Aaron and his sons have spent seven days being ordained in chapter 8. On the eighth day they offer their first sacrifices, and fire from the LORD burns up the offering on the altar. Chapter 10 follows right away with a tragedy.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Tells Aaron what to offer on the eighth day.

keyFigures.name: Aaron
keyFigures.role: Offers the first sacrifices and blesses the people.

keyFigures.name: Aaron's sons
keyFigures.role: Bring him the blood of the offerings.

keyFigures.name: The elders and the people
keyFigures.role: Bring their offerings and fall on their faces when the fire comes.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Shows his glory and sends fire to burn up the offering.

keyThemes.explanation: Aaron offers for his own sin before he offers for the people.
The priests offer the people's sacrifices, and Aaron blesses them.
The glory of the LORD appears, and fire burns up the offering.

Leviticus 10.summary: Aaron’s sons Nadab and Abihu offer "strange fire" before the LORD, which he had not commanded, and fire consumes them (Leviticus 10:1–3). Moses gives instructions on mourning and priestly service; God forbids priests from drinking wine or strong drink when entering the tent and charges them to distinguish holy from common and clean from unclean (Leviticus 10:4–11). Moses then discusses priestly portions with Aaron, who explains why the sin offering was not eaten; Moses accepts his response (Leviticus 10:12–20).
Leviticus 10.whereWeAre: The priests began their work in chapter 9, and God's fire consumed their offering. Now two of Aaron's sons offer "strange fire" (Leviticus 10:1) and die. God then tells the priests to teach the difference between clean and unclean, which chapters 11–15 explain.

keyFigures.name: Nadab and Abihu
keyFigures.role: Aaron's sons, who offer "strange fire" and die.

keyFigures.name: Aaron
keyFigures.role: Holds his peace at their death and later explains why the sin offering was not eaten.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Tells Aaron what the LORD has said and gives orders for the bodies and the offerings.

keyFigures.name: Eleazar and Ithamar
keyFigures.role: Aaron's other sons, who keep serving as priests.

keyFigures.name: Mishael and Elzaphan
keyFigures.role: Aaron's cousins, who carry the bodies out of the camp.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Sends the fire and tells the priests not to drink wine before serving.

keyThemes.explanation: God says, "I will be sanctified in them that come nigh me."
Priests must teach the difference between holy and unholy, clean and unclean.
Priests may not drink wine or strong drink before they serve.
In his grief, Aaron does not eat the sin offering, and Moses accepts his reason.

Leviticus 11.summary: The LORD tells Moses and Aaron which land animals, water creatures, birds, and swarming creatures Israelites may eat (Leviticus 11:1–23). Contact with carcasses also causes ritual uncleanness in specified circumstances (Leviticus 11:24–40). The chapter closes with God’s call to be holy and to distinguish clean from unclean, grounding these rules in the LORD who brought Israel out of Egypt (Leviticus 11:41–47).
Leviticus 11.whereWeAre: In chapter 10 God told the priests to teach the difference between clean and unclean. Chapters 11–15 spell out what that means, starting with which animals Israel may eat. Chapter 12 turns to childbirth.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Speaks these laws to Moses from the tabernacle.

keyFigures.name: Moses and Aaron
keyFigures.role: Receive the laws of clean and unclean animals.

keyThemes.explanation: God says, "ye shall therefore be holy, for I am holy."
Even what Israel eats marks them as God's people.
Touching a dead animal makes a person unclean for a while.

explainedReferences.explanation: The command to be holy because God is holy.

Leviticus 12.summary: The LORD explains the mother’s period of ritual impurity and purification following the birth of a son or daughter (Leviticus 12:1–5). Once the prescribed time is complete, she brings a lamb and bird offering; if she cannot afford a lamb, two birds are permitted (Leviticus 12:6–8). The priest makes atonement, and she is declared clean. These rules bring a mother back into the sanctuary's worship after giving birth.
Leviticus 12.whereWeAre: Chapter 11 dealt with uncleanness from food and dead animals. This short chapter explains how a mother returns to worship after giving birth. Chapters 13–14 turn to skin diseases.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Speaks these laws to Moses from the tabernacle.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Hears the LORD's words and passes them on to Israel.

keyThemes.explanation: After giving birth, a mother stays away from the sanctuary for a set time.
An offering brings her back into the worship of the tabernacle.
A family that cannot afford a lamb may bring two birds, as Mary did (Luke 2:24).

Leviticus 13.summary: God directs Moses and Aaron concerning priests’ examinations of skin swellings, eruptions, burns, and other marks (Leviticus 13:1–46). The priest may isolate and reexamine a person, pronounce someone clean, or declare a persistent condition unclean. Similar inspection rules apply to suspicious marks on clothing and leather (Leviticus 13:47–59). Careful checking protects both the person and the camp.
Leviticus 13.whereWeAre: The laws on clean and unclean continue from chapters 11–12. This chapter explains how a priest checks skin diseases, and even mold on clothing, to decide what is unclean. Chapter 14 explains how a healed person is made clean again.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Speaks these laws to Moses from the tabernacle.

keyFigures.name: Moses and Aaron
keyFigures.role: Receive the laws for skin diseases.

keyFigures.name: The priest
keyFigures.role: Looks at the skin and the clothing and declares them clean or unclean.

keyThemes.explanation: The priest waits and looks again before he decides.
A person with the disease lives outside the camp and cries, "Unclean, unclean."
Mold in cloth or leather is also checked.

Leviticus 14.summary: The LORD gives a restoration ceremony for a person healed of leprosy, involving two birds, cedar, scarlet yarn, hyssop, washing, shaving, and later sacrifices (Leviticus 14:1–32). Lower-cost offerings are allowed for those with limited means. The chapter also gives procedures for examining, treating, or demolishing a house with spreading marks once Israel inhabits Canaan (Leviticus 14:33–53), concluding the laws for such conditions (Leviticus 14:54–57).
Leviticus 14.whereWeAre: Chapter 13 explained how a priest decides that a skin disease makes a person unclean. This chapter explains how someone who has healed is welcomed back, and how to deal with mold in a house once Israel lives in Canaan. Chapter 15 finishes the clean and unclean laws.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Speaks these laws to Moses from the tabernacle.

keyFigures.name: Moses and Aaron
keyFigures.role: Receive the laws for cleansing the healed and checking houses.

keyFigures.name: The priest
keyFigures.role: Goes outside the camp to check the healed person and later checks the house.

keyThemes.explanation: A ceremony with two birds brings the healed person back into the camp.
A poor person may bring smaller offerings.
Houses in Canaan are also checked for spreading mold.

Leviticus 15.summary: Rules address abnormal male discharges, emission of semen, menstruation, and prolonged female bleeding (Leviticus 15:1–30). Washing, waiting until evening, and in some cases offerings provide the path back to cleanness. The concluding verses link these distinctions to protection of the tabernacle from uncleanness (Leviticus 15:31–33). These are temporary conditions of being unclean, not sins.
Leviticus 15.whereWeAre: This is the last of the clean and unclean laws in chapters 11–15. It covers discharges from the body, both normal and unusual. With these rules in place, chapter 16 describes the one day each year when the whole people and the sanctuary are cleansed.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Speaks these laws to Moses from the tabernacle.

keyFigures.name: Moses and Aaron
keyFigures.role: Receive the laws for discharges from the body.

keyThemes.explanation: Normal events of the body make a person unclean for a time.
Washing, waiting, and sometimes an offering make a person clean again.
These laws keep uncleanness away from the tabernacle.

Leviticus 16.summary: After the deaths of Aaron’s sons, the LORD limits access to the most holy place and gives Aaron a solemn annual procedure (Leviticus 16:1–5). He makes sin offerings for himself and the people, sprinkles blood within the most holy place, and sends away a live goat, the scapegoat, carrying Israel's confessed sins (Leviticus 16:6–28). The people must humble themselves and cease work on the appointed annual day (Leviticus 16:29–34). Once a year, this day cleanses the sanctuary and the whole people from their sins.
Leviticus 16.whereWeAre: This chapter takes us back to the death of Aaron's two sons in chapter 10. To keep that from happening again, God explains when and how the high priest may enter the most holy place. He may go in only once a year, on the Day of Atonement, and then chapters 17–27 turn to holy living.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Tells Aaron when and how he may come into the most holy place.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Hears the LORD's words and passes them on to Israel.

keyFigures.name: Aaron
keyFigures.role: Offers for himself and the people and confesses Israel's sins over the scapegoat.

keyFigures.name: The man who leads the goat
keyFigures.role: Takes the scapegoat into the wilderness.

keyThemes.explanation: The high priest makes atonement for himself, the people, and the sanctuary.
Aaron may not come behind the veil whenever he wants.
The scapegoat carries the people's sins into the wilderness.
The day is kept every year as "a statute for ever."

Leviticus 17.summary: The LORD directs Israelites to bring certain sacrificial slaughter to the sanctuary rather than offer sacrifices in the open field, and never to offer sacrifices "unto devils" (Leviticus 17:1–9). Eating blood is prohibited for Israelites and resident foreigners, because blood represents life and is given for altar atonement (Leviticus 17:10–14). Rules also address animals found dead or torn by beasts (Leviticus 17:15–16). The chapter ties worship and respect for life together.
Leviticus 17.whereWeAre: The Day of Atonement in chapter 16 dealt with sin at the sanctuary. Chapters 17–26 turn to holy living in everyday life, starting here with where sacrifices may be made and why blood must not be eaten: "the life of the flesh is in the blood" (Leviticus 17:11). Chapter 18 moves on to sexual purity.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Speaks these laws to Moses from the tabernacle.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Hears the LORD's words and passes them on to Israel.

keyFigures.name: Aaron and his sons
keyFigures.role: Are told that every sacrifice must be brought to the tabernacle.

keyThemes.explanation: Sacrifices must be brought to the tabernacle, not offered to "devils" in the fields.
Blood must not be eaten, because "the life of the flesh is in the blood."
God has given the blood on the altar to make atonement.

Leviticus 18.summary: God warns Israel not to imitate the practices attributed to Egypt or Canaan and commands obedience to his statutes (Leviticus 18:1–5). The chapter prohibits specified incestuous relationships, intercourse during menstruation, offering children to Molech, male same-sex intercourse, and sexual relations with animals (Leviticus 18:6–23). It warns that the land and its inhabitants are defiled by such practices and that Israel must not repeat them (Leviticus 18:24–30).
Leviticus 18.whereWeAre: Chapter 17 began the laws about holy living with rules on blood and sacrifice. This chapter turns to family and sexual life, telling Israel not to live like Egypt, which they left, or Canaan, where they are going. Chapter 19 widens the call to holiness to every part of life.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Tells Israel, "I am the LORD your God," and forbids the ways of Egypt and Canaan.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Hears the LORD's words and passes them on to Israel.

keyThemes.explanation: Israel must not live like Egypt or Canaan.
God forbids sexual relations with close relatives and other sins.
For these sins "the land itself vomiteth out her inhabitants."

explainedReferences.explanation: Statement that the person who does these things will live by them.
Statement that the person who does these things will live by them.

Leviticus 19.summary: The LORD calls the whole congregation to be holy because he is holy (Leviticus 19:1–2). Commands address parents, Sabbath, idolatry, proper worship, gleaning for the poor, honesty, fair wages, disability, justice, slander, vengeance, and love of neighbor (Leviticus 19:3–18). Further laws concern mixed materials, sexual misconduct, divination, bodily customs, respect for elders, fair treatment of foreigners, and honest measures (Leviticus 19:19–37). Holiness shows up in how people treat each other every day.
Leviticus 19.whereWeAre: Chapter 18 dealt with sexual purity. Now God says, "Ye shall be holy: for I the LORD your God am holy" (Leviticus 19:2), and shows what that looks like in daily life. This chapter includes "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself" (Leviticus 19:18), which Jesus later calls the second great commandment (Matthew 22:39).

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Calls the whole congregation to be holy because he is holy.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Hears the LORD's words and passes them on to Israel.

keyThemes.explanation: Holiness covers worship, family, and daily life.
"thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." Jesus calls this the second great commandment.

keyThemes.theme: Care for the poor and the stranger
keyThemes.explanation: Farmers leave food for the poor, and strangers are to be loved as one's own.
Workers must be paid the same day, and weights must be fair.

explainedReferences.explanation: The command to be holy because God is holy.
The command to love one's neighbor as oneself is directly quoted.
The command to love your neighbor as yourself.

Leviticus 20.summary: The LORD states penalties for giving offspring to Molech and for consulting mediums or spiritists (Leviticus 20:1–8; Leviticus 20:27). Other provisions address cursing parents and prohibited sexual relationships, often with severe sanctions or exclusion from the people (Leviticus 20:9–21). The chapter closes by linking obedience, separation from surrounding peoples, and possession of the land (Leviticus 20:22–26). Serious penalties protect Israel's holiness as God's people.
Leviticus 20.whereWeAre: Chapters 18–19 listed many sins Israel must avoid. This chapter gives the penalties for them, including worshiping Molech and consulting mediums. Chapters 21–22 turn to the priests, who must live by even stricter rules.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Sets the penalties for the worst sins and calls Israel to be his own.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Hears the LORD's words and passes them on to Israel.

keyThemes.explanation: The worst sins bring the death penalty.
Israel must not give children to Molech or turn to mediums.
God says he has "severed you from other people, that ye should be mine."

explainedReferences.explanation: Moses' instruction that the person who curses father or mother must die.
The penalty against cursing father or mother.

Leviticus 21.summary: The LORD gives priests special rules concerning contact with the dead, mourning practices, and marriage (Leviticus 21:1–9). The high priest faces stricter restrictions (Leviticus 21:10–15). Descendants of Aaron with specified physical conditions may eat holy food but may not approach to offer the food of God at the altar (Leviticus 21:16–24). Those who serve closest to God's presence have the strictest rules.
Leviticus 21.whereWeAre: Chapters 17–20 called all Israel to be holy. Chapters 21–22 set even higher standards for the priests, who serve closest to God. This chapter covers their mourning, their marriages, and who may offer at the altar.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Speaks these laws to Moses from the tabernacle.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Tells the priests, the sons of Aaron, the rules for their office.

keyThemes.explanation: Priests must be holy because they offer "the bread of their God."
The high priest has the strictest rules of all.
A priest with a blemish may not serve at the altar, but he still eats the holy food.

Leviticus 22.summary: God instructs Aaron’s priestly household not to handle or eat holy contributions while ritually unclean (Leviticus 22:1–9). Detailed rules define who in a priest’s household may eat sacred food and what happens if an outsider eats it unintentionally (Leviticus 22:10–16). The chapter then requires unblemished animals for vows and freewill offerings and specifies additional conditions for newborn animals and thanksgiving sacrifices (Leviticus 22:17–33).
Leviticus 22.whereWeAre: Chapter 21 gave rules for the priests themselves. This chapter covers how they handle holy food and which animals may be offered. With the priests' rules complete, chapter 23 turns to Israel's yearly calendar of feasts.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Speaks these laws to Moses from the tabernacle.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Hears the LORD's words and passes them on to Israel.

keyFigures.name: Aaron and his sons
keyFigures.role: Are told to treat the holy things with care.

keyThemes.explanation: The priests' food is holy and must not be treated as ordinary.
Animals offered must be without blemish.
"Neither shall ye profane my holy name."

Leviticus 23.summary: The LORD gives Israel his feasts, starting with the weekly Sabbath (Leviticus 23:1–3). In spring come the Passover and seven days of unleavened bread (Leviticus 23:4–8), then the waving of the first sheaf of the harvest (Leviticus 23:9–14). Fifty days later a new grain offering is brought, and the corners of the field are left for the poor and the stranger (Leviticus 23:15–22). In the seventh month come the blowing of trumpets (Leviticus 23:23–25), the day of atonement (Leviticus 23:26–32), and the feast of tabernacles, when Israel lives in booths to remember the wilderness (Leviticus 23:33–44).
Leviticus 23.whereWeAre: The priests' rules were given in chapters 21–22. Now God lays out Israel's holy calendar: the Sabbath and the yearly feasts, from Passover to the feast of tabernacles. Chapter 24 adds rules for the daily care of the tabernacle.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Gives Israel his feasts.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Declares the feasts to the children of Israel.

keyThemes.explanation: The Sabbath and the feasts give Israel's year its shape.
Passover and the feast of tabernacles recall how God brought Israel out of Egypt.
The first sheaf and the offering fifty days later thank God for the harvest.
Even among the feast laws, Israel must leave gleanings for the poor and the stranger.

Leviticus 24.summary: The Israelites are to supply pure olive oil for the continually tended sanctuary lamps, and Aaron is to arrange twelve loaves on the sacred table each Sabbath (Leviticus 24:1–9). A man described as the son of an Israelite woman and an Egyptian father blasphemes the name of the LORD; he is held until the LORD’s judgment is known, then executed by the community (Leviticus 24:10–16; Leviticus 24:23). The chapter also states rules for homicide, animal damage, and bodily injury (Leviticus 24:17–22).
Leviticus 24.whereWeAre: Chapter 23 set Israel's yearly feasts. This chapter turns to the lamp and bread kept in the tabernacle at all times, then tells of a man who curses God's name. His case leads to laws on injury, including "eye for eye" (Leviticus 24:20), before chapter 25 turns to the land.

Leviticus 25.summary: On Mount Sinai the LORD commands a seventh-year rest for farmland and vineyards (Leviticus 25:1–7). After seven cycles of seven years, the fiftieth year is declared Jubilee, associated with liberty, family property returns, and special cultivation restrictions (Leviticus 25:8–22). Laws govern valuation and redemption of land and homes, aid to the poor, loans, and the treatment and redemption of Israelites who enter servitude (Leviticus 25:23–55). The chapter teaches that the land ultimately belongs to God.
Leviticus 25.whereWeAre: Chapter 23 set Israel's weekly and yearly holy days. This chapter adds rest for the land every seventh year and a Jubilee every fiftieth year, when Israel must "proclaim liberty throughout all the land" (Leviticus 25:10) and land returns to its families. It looks ahead to life in Canaan and leads into the blessings and warnings of chapter 26.

Leviticus 26.summary: The LORD forbids idols and commands respect for his Sabbaths and sanctuary (Leviticus 26:1–2). If Israel obeys, the text promises agricultural plenty, security, peace, and God’s presence (Leviticus 26:3–13). Persistent disobedience brings escalating warnings of hunger, defeat, devastation, exile, and desolated land (Leviticus 26:14–39). Yet confession, humbled hearts, and God’s remembrance of the covenant hold out hope (Leviticus 26:40–46).
Leviticus 26.whereWeAre: The laws God gave at Sinai in Leviticus are almost done. In this chapter God sets out the blessings Israel will enjoy if they obey and the punishments if they do not, all the way to exile. It ends with hope, and chapter 27 adds a closing note on vows.

Leviticus 27.summary: The LORD supplies valuations for persons vowed to the sanctuary, adjusted for age and sex with allowance for the poor (Leviticus 27:1–8). Further rules cover dedicated animals, houses, and fields, including redemption payments; firstborn animals already belonging to the LORD cannot be dedicated as though they were an additional gift (Leviticus 27:9–27). The chapter closes with rules about devoted things and tithes, and identifies the laws as commands given to Moses for Israel at Sinai (Leviticus 27:28–34).
Leviticus 27.whereWeAre: Chapter 26 reads like an ending, with its blessings and warnings. This last chapter adds rules for vows and gifts given to the LORD. Leviticus closes at Sinai, and Numbers picks up one month after the tabernacle was set up, with Israel getting ready to leave.
